blurb: Open versus closed models, who the major labs are, the DeepSeek shock and how AI makes money.

cards.title: Two ways to ship a model

steps.p: Models like GPT, Claude and Gemini are used through an API or app. The weights never leave the company.
Models like Llama, Mistral, Qwen and DeepSeek publish their weights for anyone to download, run and modify.
Most open-weight releases withhold training data and full code, and many carry license restrictions.

cards.aside: The Open Source Initiative published a formal definition of open-source AI in 2024 that most open-weight models do not meet.

options: Open source also requires enough information about training data and the code to reproduce the model
Open weights are free; open source is paid
cards.why: Reproducibility. Weights let you run and fine-tune a model. Open source in the traditional sense means you could study and rebuild it.

cards.statement: Meta's Llama models qualify as open source under the Open Source Initiative's definition.
cards.why: False. Llama's license includes restrictions — for example, very large companies need a separate license — and training data is not disclosed.

cards.q: A main reason a company might pick an open-weight model is to…
options: Run it privately on its own servers and customize it without vendor lock-in
cards.why: Control. Sensitive data never leaves your infrastructure, you can fine-tune freely, and you are not exposed to a provider's price or policy changes.

cards.title: Meta's first LLaMA model leaked onto the internet within about a week of its limited release in 2023.
cards.detail: Meta had shared it only with approved researchers. The leak spread via 4chan and kicked off a wave of open experimentation — and Meta later chose to release its models openly.

cards.statement: The best open-weight models have generally trailed the best closed models by around a year or less.
cards.why: True. Analyses such as Epoch AI's estimated the gap at roughly a year, and releases like DeepSeek-R1 narrowed it to months at times.

cards.title: Who builds frontier AI

steps.p: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta and xAI lead in frontier models, with Microsoft, Amazon and Google supplying much of the computing.
DeepSeek, Alibaba's Qwen team, Moonshot and others release strong models, many with open weights.
France's Mistral AI is Europe's best-known model maker.

cards.aside: A handful of organizations account for nearly all frontier-scale training runs.

options: Former OpenAI researchers, including Dario and Daniela Amodei
cards.why: Ex-OpenAI researchers. The founders focused the company on AI safety research alongside building frontier models like Claude.

cards.statement: OpenAI was founded in 2015 as a nonprofit.
cards.why: True. It added a "capped-profit" company in 2019 to raise capital, and its structure has been restructured and debated since.

cards.q: In 2023, Google merged two AI groups to form Google DeepMind. They were…
cards.why: Google Brain and DeepMind. Brain (where the transformer was invented) and London-based DeepMind (AlphaGo) combined under Demis Hassabis.

cards.title: DeepSeek is funded by High-Flyer, a Chinese quantitative hedge fund.
cards.detail: The fund had stockpiled GPUs for trading research. Founder Liang Wenfeng spun out DeepSeek in 2023 to pursue general AI.

cards.statement: Mistral AI is headquartered in France.
cards.why: True. Founded in Paris in 2023 by former Google DeepMind and Meta researchers, it releases both open-weight and commercial models.

cards.title: January 2025

steps.p: DeepSeek released R1, an open-weight reasoning model that rivaled OpenAI's o1 on many benchmarks.
A widely quoted figure put the training cost of its base model at about $5.6 million — a fraction of what rivals were assumed to spend.
On January 27, NVIDIA lost about $590 billion in market value in a single day, the largest one-day loss in US market history.

cards.aside: Within weeks, the stock had recovered much of the drop as analysts reassessed.

cards.statement: DeepSeek's ~$5.6 million figure covered the full cost of developing the model.
cards.why: False. It covered GPU rental time for the final training run of V3 only — not research, failed experiments, staff, data or the hardware itself. Total costs were far higher.

cards.q: Why did cheap-training claims rattle chip stocks?
options: They suggested AI might need far less spending on GPUs than expected
cards.why: Demand fears. Investors worried that efficient training would reduce the need for enormous GPU purchases.

cards.q: The Jevons paradox suggests that making AI cheaper to run might…
options: Increase total demand, as cheaper AI gets used far more
cards.why: Efficiency can raise consumption. Jevons observed that more efficient steam engines increased coal use. Many argued cheaper AI would expand usage enough to raise GPU demand.

cards.title: DeepSeek released R1's weights under the permissive MIT license.
cards.detail: That allowed anyone to use, modify and commercialize it with almost no restrictions, and it quickly appeared on major cloud platforms.

cards.statement: DeepSeek's app briefly became the top free app on Apple's US App Store.
cards.why: True. In late January 2025 it overtook ChatGPT in the App Store rankings, a striking moment for a little-known Chinese lab.

cards.title: The economics

steps.p: Huge up-front training costs, then ongoing inference costs for every user query.
Consumer subscriptions, per-token API pricing for developers, and enterprise contracts.
The price of a given level of capability has dropped dramatically, as competition and efficiency improve.

cards.aside: Cloud providers profit either way, by selling the computing that all of this runs on.

cards.q: How has the price of reaching a fixed capability level, like GPT-4-class performance, changed since 2023?
cards.why: Collapsed. Analyses such as Epoch AI's found prices for a given performance level falling between roughly 10× and several hundred times per year, depending on the task.

cards.statement: ChatGPT reached an estimated 100 million users about two months after launch.
cards.why: True, according to a widely cited UBS analysis in early 2023 — then the fastest-growing consumer app on record.

cards.q: Which two cloud giants made major investments in Anthropic?
cards.why: Amazon and Google. Microsoft, by contrast, is OpenAI's biggest backer. These deals tie labs to the clouds that supply their compute.

cards.title: ChatGPT launched on November 30, 2022, as a "low-key research preview".
cards.detail: OpenAI staff reportedly expected modest interest. It reached a million users in five days and triggered the generative AI boom.

cards.title: Read the source, not the headline
cards.body: AI news is distorted fast. A model's own announcement, paper or system card tells you what was claimed, how it was measured, and what the limits are.
cards.challenge: Pick one AI announcement from this week and read the original post instead of a summary of it.
